about: Prepared answers, dev split, judged by gpt-5.6-luna (foundry, inline): written by the MLflow run 'judge gpt-5.6-luna · foundry inline · prepared answers dev-sample-302' in experiment 'daily-drill'. Endpoint and resource names are left out on purpose.

params.split_rule: lessons dealt 60/20/20 within each phase, frozen in prepared_splits.json

answers.notes: It inaccurately says output tokens are the words the model writes, whereas the lesson says a token is roughly three quarters of a word.

It overstates the evidence by saying retrieval did its job identically and that retrieval settings cannot explain the change; the traces show only that the same set of articles was sent, so they point first to generation rather than ruling retrieval out completely.
It introduces unsupported claims about Azure VM billing, identity fields, and Azure Cost Management, and uses unexplained jargon such as Pydantic and Spacelift.
It incorrectly implies that looking up old IDs necessarily requires shared state; an explicit read or join could perform a lookup, although Spark will not do it automatically.
It incorrectly says an empty quarantine table usually means the checks are not running, when it could simply mean no rows violated the contract.
It makes an unsupported claim that ai_mask uses a named-entity-recognition approach, which the lesson does not establish.
It adds unsupported claims about embedding-model input limits and text being cut off, which are not stated in the lesson.
It overstates that unchanged request volume means each request used more tokens, overlooking that prices or the model mix could also have changed.
It adds unsupported claims that force-unlocking makes state lose track of resources and that Azure blob history will show two writes, neither of which the lesson establishes.
It inaccurately says the unsupported claim is a statement “nobody checked,” even though the verifier did check it and found it unsupported.
The plan can be empty for reasons other than dropping, such as the effective provider value already being unchanged, and a field need not appear specifically in runbook locals to be passed onward.
It incorrectly assumes output was already the bigger part of the cost, which the lesson does not guarantee.
It is clear and accurate, but it includes mathematical notation such as "% 100" and percentages despite the plain-words requirement.
It uses multiplication symbols and equations despite the requirement for plain words without maths notation.
It contradicts the strict gate by saying not to shelve an idea that lacks past examples with right answers, even though the lesson says any failed gate means shelve.
It uses unexplained jargon such as Pydantic and workspace policy, so it is not fully plain for beginners.
It claims command-line and environment values override target values, but the lesson only establishes that target values override defaults and does not state that precedence.
It overstates that every path must map to an external location, whereas the lesson says a path can have no covering location.
It incorrectly says LangChain passes `Answer {question}` to the model, whereas doubled braces are kept as literal text, so the result should still contain `{{question}}`.
It overstates that a two-point drop is noise; the lesson only says a one-point drop on 100 questions never passes, so larger gaps must be judged with the paired check.
It uses unexplained technical terms such as “trace,” “token_usage,” and “system.ai_gateway.usage,” which is not fully plain for beginners.

The claim that each layer needs its own permission is too broad: Unity Catalog privileges can be granted at different levels and inherited, rather than every catalog, schema, and table each requiring a separate permission.
It overstates that catalog-level EXECUTE would let the service principal run the function, since USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are also required.
It overstates that overlap gives the model no extra emphasis, since both overlapping chunks could be retrieved and included in the prompt.
It uses unexplained jargon such as “flaky,” “pass@3,” “pass^3,” and “MLflow,” so it is not fully plain.
It overclaims that past refunds are examples with right answers; historical refund records are not necessarily correct labeled decisions, so this gate is not established.
It asserts without support from the lesson that cluster tags are copied into usage rows and that account budgets can be filtered by a tag.
It incorrectly says classifier scores are numbers between 0 and 1, which the lesson does not state.
It uses unexplained jargon such as “reranker,” “paired check,” and “LLM,” so it is not fully plain for beginners.
It says a prompt pasted into code was edited even though no code changed, which is internally contradictory and not supported by the lesson.
It wrongly presents the commit as the only missing piece, overlooking that a good prompt also identifies the run and provides the repository as well as the first error and commit.

It incorrectly claims that fixed costs are usually well known and that a guess already known well has a small swing; the lesson defines swing by changing a guess from bad to good, not by how certain the guess is.
It incorrectly suggests dividing by the smaller of k and the number of relevant documents, which changes the lesson's recall definition and can make an incomplete result appear perfect.
The documents-that-change and very-large-data sections exceed the requested two or three sentences each.
The large-store suggestion to fetch only expired memories would miss recent memories belonging to people who asked to be forgotten, unless those deletion requests are handled separately.
It makes unsupported claims that the comparison order is random and that later cases repeat the same causes, neither of which is stated in the lesson.
It misleadingly calls ship and keep the baseline the two firm answers, although the lesson defines three decisions, including too close to call.
It overclaims that processing only new documents will stay fast and cheap however big the table gets, which the lesson does not guarantee.
It incorrectly recasts the lesson's request-level 0.6% failure rate as 0.6% of users, which the lesson does not establish.
It adds the unsupported detail that the discount may be agreed with Microsoft; the lesson only says a discount may have been agreed.
It uses the mathematical notation “60/20/20,” which conflicts with the plain-language requirement to avoid maths notation.
It overstates the benefit by saying the job stays small and cheap no matter how large the table grows, and incorrectly says speed was never the issue.
It incorrectly says rollback is appropriate when the new version has fewer passes, instead of comparing pass rates, which can differ when versions have different numbers of traces.
It incorrectly says CAN_USE is required on the endpoint, while the lesson allows either CAN_USE or CAN_MANAGE.

It adds workspace bindings, row filters, masks, and authoritative Terraform behavior that are not in the lesson, and its first point contradicts the lesson's claim that the three checks determine access.
It uses unexplained jargon such as “deployment's quota,” “gateway's rate limits,” and “go-live,” so it is not fully plain for beginners.
It is clear and accurate but includes the mathematical/code notation `% 100`, which conflicts with the plain-language requirement.
It asserts that output tokens usually cost more than input tokens, but the lesson gives no such pricing fact, so that claim is unsupported under the stated source of truth.
It incorrectly presents USE SCHEMA on the schema as required, omitting that USE SCHEMA granted on the catalog also suffices through inheritance.
It incorrectly says different text gives different hash numbers, since distinct inputs can sometimes share a hash bucket.
It incorrectly says doubled braces may reach the model; in LangChain, doubled braces are escaping syntax and should produce single braces in the rendered prompt.
It uses division symbols such as “$5 ÷ 8” despite the requirement to avoid maths notation.
It overstates the ordering rule by saying a running stack must wait for every stack it depends on, omitting the lesson's qualification that a dependency only matters if it is running too.
It overstates the role of success rate: the earning side also includes volume and value per success, so success rate is a factor in that side, not exactly the whole earning half.

It overstates that a contradiction means the surrounding claims cannot be trusted; the lesson requires abstaining because any contradiction triggers that safe policy, while other claims may still be individually supported.
The claim that a lock is only released by the run that took it is too absolute, because an operator can remove a stale lock with force-unlock after confirming the run is dead.
It incorrectly says that changing what the function returns updates the shown tool schema, which the lesson describes as the name, description, and input parameters.
The first situation introduces group names containing '@', which conflicts with the lesson's stated model that groups have plain names and the marker reliably distinguishes them from people.
It incorrectly says renaming managed_resource_group_name should produce only an in-place change, even though the lesson says that change forces replacement.
The claim that plain `terraform init` will print an installation line for comparison is unreliable; the committed lock file is the dependable check for the exact provider version.
It adds unsupported claims that a bigger model might help slightly and that it costs more and is slower.
It adds the unsupported claim that using a supervisor would incur extra cost and provide no gain.

The claim that a plan cannot distinguish a resource reference from a typed-in value is wrong: an unresolved resource reference can appear as an unknown value, while a literal value can be shown directly.
It overstates the behavior by saying a token bucket sends requests at a steady rate and prevents 429s altogether, even though the lesson says it permits short bursts and helps avoid 429s.
It adds claims about prevent_destroy and Spacelift policies that are not supported by the lesson and overstates that prevent_destroy stops any plan that would destroy the resource.
The claim that using the same user hash makes one test's effects pile onto the next is not established by the lesson; repeated assignment alone does not cause that.
It adds the unsupported claim that one day cannot show weekly patterns, which is not stated in the lesson.
The claim that a falling kappa with steady AC1 points to rarer failures rather than a worse judge is too strong, since the scores alone do not establish that cause.
